The '''Brusselator''' is a theoretical model for a type of [[autocatalytic reaction]].
The Brusselator model was proposed by [[Ilya Prigogine]] and his collaborators at the [[Université Libre de Bruxelles]].<ref>{{cite web
| url = http://www.idea.wsu.edu/OscilChem/#Brusselator%20Model
| title = IDEA - Internet Differential Equations Activities
| publisher = [[Washington State University]]
| accessdate = 2010-05-16
| archive-date = 2017-09-09
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170909182522/http://www.idea.wsu.edu/OscilChem/#Brusselator%20Model
| url-status = dead
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Prigogine |first1=I. |last2=Lefever |first2=R. |date=1968-02-15 |title=Symmetry Breaking Instabilities in Dissipative Systems. II |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jcp/article/48/4/1695/83930/Symmetry-Breaking-Instabilities-in-Dissipative |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=1695–1700 |doi=10.1063/1.1668896 |bibcode=1968JChPh..48.1695P |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It is a portmanteau of [[Brussels]] and [[oscillator]].

It is characterized by the reactions

:<math>  A \rightarrow X</math>

:<math>  2X + Y \rightarrow 3X</math>

:<math>  B + X \rightarrow Y + D</math>

:<math>  X \rightarrow E</math>

Under conditions where A and B are in vast excess and can thus be modeled at constant concentration, the rate equations become

:<math>{d \over dt}\left[ X \right] = \left[A \right] + \left[ X \right]^2 \left[Y \right]  - \left[B \right] \left[X \right] - \left[X \right]  \,</math>

:<math>{d \over dt}\left[ Y \right] =   \left[B \right] \left[X \right] - \left[ X \right]^2 \left[Y \right]    \,</math>

where, for convenience, the rate constants have been set to 1.

The Brusselator has a fixed point at

:<math>\left[ X \right] =   \left[ A \right]    \,</math>

:<math>\left[ Y \right] =   {\left[ B \right] \over \left[ A \right]}    \,</math>.

The fixed point becomes unstable when

:<math> \left[ B \right]>1+\left[ A \right]^2   \,</math>

leading to an oscillation of the system. Unlike the [[Lotka–Volterra]] equation, the oscillations of the Brusselator do not depend on the amount of reactant present initially. Instead, after sufficient time, the oscillations approach a [[limit cycle]].<ref>[http://www.bibliotecapleyades.net/archivos_pdf/brusselator.pdf Dynamics of the Brusselator]
</ref>

The best-known example is a [[chemical clock]], such as the [[Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction]] (BZ reaction). It can be created with a mixture of potassium bromate (KBrO<sub>3</sub>), malonic acid (CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub>), and manganese sulfate (MnSO<sub>4</sub>) prepared in a heated solution of [[sulfuric acid]] (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>).<ref>[http://online.redwoods.cc.ca.us/instruct/darnold/deproj/Sp98/Gabe/ BZ reaction] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121231011212/http://online.redwoods.cc.ca.us/instruct/darnold/deproj/Sp98/Gabe/ |date=December 31, 2012 }}</ref>
